newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Prospects rise for deal on Hebron on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Prospects rise for deal on Hebron on Tuesday.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians, nudged forward by U.N. President Bill Clinton's Middle East envoy, neared the goal of sealing a deal before New Year's Day on the long-delayed Israeli pullout from the West Bank town of Hebron.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, speaking after talks with U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, said he hoped to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later on Tuesday to sign an agreement on a withdrawal.
The Arab world regards an accord on Hebron as an acid test of the hardline Israeli prime minister's intentions.
Arafat, asked if he would meet Netanyahu later in the day to sign an accord, told reporters: "We hope so. If everything goes smoothly we can have this opportunity."
An Israeli negotiator who declined to be identified mirrored Arafat's optimism, saying he was "anticipating a Netanyahu-Arafat meeting taking place on Tuesday to sign a deal."

Ross arrived from Washington late on Monday and met Netanyahu in Jerusalem and Arafat in Gaza to press for swift agreement on the pullout from Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns due for self-rule under Israeli-PLO peace accords.
Arafat said of the negotiators: "They are working through issues that are complex and in very great detail. They are working hard."
He declined to go into details, but said talks would continue on Tuesday morning.
Palestinian negotiator Mohammad Dahlan said earlier a troop redeployment in Hebron would take place within a week.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiators have held marathon sessions to nail down final details of a troop withdrawal from 80 percent of Hebron, the West Bank flashpoint from which the Jewish state should to have pulled back last March.
Netanyahu's predecessor, Shimon Peres, froze the planned withdrawal in response to Islamic suicide bombings that killed 59 people in the Jewish state in February and March.
Netanyahu ousted Peres in an upset election victory in May and talks foundered over his demands for greater security for the 400 Jewish settlers living in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.
The negotiations were moribund until Clinton ordered Ross to the region to breathe new life into them earlier this month. A previous Ross peace mission had collapsed in October.

Ross's success in bringing the two sides together, highlighted by a Netanyahu-Arafat meeting at the Israel-Gaza border a week ago, alarmed settlers fearful that the hawkish government they helped to elect in May was selling them out.
Settler jitters were underscored late on Monday when a member of Kfar Darom settlement in the Gaza Strip shot dead a Palestinian who had entered the isolated enclave.
"The preliminary investigation indicates the victim carried neither weapons nor documents," said an Israeli military source.
The source said the settler called on the Palestinian to stop "and when the man did not respond the settler opened fire, first at his legs, then at his body."
A second settler who saw the shooting said the victim "attacked" the settler before he opened fire. Police detained the settler for questioning, the military source said.

Netanyahu, mindful of a mounting right-wing backlash, vowed on Monday he would sign a deal only if it guaranteed the safety of Hebron's settlers and of the Cave of the Patriarchs, a site holy to both Jews and Moslems.

But Netanyahu, at times fiercely defiant, can little afford to ignore the policy concerns of Washington, Israel's crucial ally, which views a Hebron withdrawal as critical to the future of the wider Middle East peace process.
